questions.question: What is the 'core idea' behind all coding-decoding questions?
options: Find the hidden transformation rule linking input to output, then apply it to a new case
Guess based on word length only
questions.rationale: Every coding-decoding question boils down to finding the hidden rule connecting a given input to its output, then applying that same rule to a new case.

questions.question: Why are several major 'types' of coding-decoding typically distinguished (letter, number, substitution, matrix, etc.)?
options: There is really only one type
Because each type uses a fundamentally different kind of transformation rule, requiring different detection strategies
Because letter-based coding is the only type actually tested
questions.rationale: Different coding types (letter-based, number-based, substitution, matrix, etc.) use fundamentally different transformation rules, so recognizing which type applies is an important first step.

questions.question: What is the 'reverse alphabet' mapping?
options: Pairing each letter with its mirror position, so A<->Z, B<->Y, and so on
Mapping every letter to a number only
questions.rationale: Reverse alphabet coding mirrors each letter around the center of the alphabet: A pairs with Z, B with Y, and so on.

questions.question: In 'reverse alphabet vector' terms, what does a letter's reverse-alphabet partner satisfy?
questions.rationale: Since the alphabet has 26 letters, a letter at position p and its reverse-alphabet partner at position (27-p) always sum to 27.

questions.question: What is a 'fast alphabet group', as a memory aid?
options: A random cluster of unrelated letters
A memorized cluster of nearby letters and positions used to quickly compute shifts without counting from A each time
questions.rationale: Fast alphabet groups are memorized clusters of letters and their positions, used as quick mental anchors instead of counting from A every time.

questions.question: Why are 'important alphabet pairs' (like A-Z, M-N) worth memorizing?
options: They act as quick anchor points for calculating any letter's position or reverse-position rapidly
They are only used in reverse coding
questions.rationale: Key reference pairs like A-Z (1 and 26) or M-N (13 and 14, the alphabet's midpoint) provide fast anchor points for calculating other positions relative to them.

questions.question: In reverse alphabet coding, what does the letter B map to?
questions.rationale: B is position 2; its reverse-alphabet partner is at position 27-2=25, which is Y.

questions.question: In reverse alphabet coding, what does the letter M map to?
questions.rationale: M is position 13; its reverse-alphabet partner is at position 27-13=14, which is N.

questions.question: What position does the letter M occupy in the alphabet?
questions.rationale: M is the 13th letter of the alphabet.

questions.question: What position does the letter N occupy, and why does this confirm M and N are reverse-alphabet neighbors?
options: 14; because 13+14=27, matching the reverse-alphabet sum rule
15; because M and N are unrelated
13; N and M share the same position
questions.rationale: N is position 14, and since 13 (M) + 14 (N) = 27, this confirms M and N are exactly reverse-alphabet partners of each other.
